summary: Reviewed the add-timeout-flag spec. Two findings: P1 on missing cleanup of the SIGALRM handler on successful completion (handler leaks into subsequent commands in long-running shells), P2 on Windows behavior when the flag is supplied (silent no-op is surprising; should warn or error). Both map to existing tasks and do not need new BCs.

findings.title: SIGALRM handler is not cleared on successful completion
findings.what_wrong: When the CLI runs under a long-lived shell (e.g. REPL) and completes before the timeout fires, the SIGALRM handler remains installed. The next command inherits the stale handler, causing a spurious termination once the original timeout elapses.
findings.suggested_fix: Clear the alarm and restore the previous SIGALRM handler in a finally block after command dispatch completes.
findings.evidence: task t1.2 installs signal.alarm(N) but does not show signal.alarm(0) on the return path.

findings.title: Windows silent no-op is surprising
findings.what_wrong: On Windows, the platform guard skips SIGALRM installation but still accepts --timeout without warning. Users will believe timeouts are active.
findings.suggested_fix: On Windows with --timeout > 0, print a warning to stderr that the flag is unsupported on this platform.
findings.evidence: task t1.2 guard only skips installation; does not surface the no-op.

residual_risks: Very short timeouts (under 1 second) may race with handler installation; consider minimum-timeout guard in a follow-up.
